title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Seven years had passed. The storm-tossed sea of European history had subsided within its shores and seemed to have grown calm. But the mysterious forces that move humanity—mysterious because the laws governing them are unknown to us—continued to operate.

Though the surface of the sea of history appeared motionless, the movement of humanity went on as ceaselessly as the flow of time. Various groups of people formed and dissolved, the formation and dissolution of kingdoms and displacements of peoples were in preparation.

The sea of history was no longer driven violently from shore to shore as before. It was churning in its depths. Historical figures were no longer carried by the waves from one shore to another. They now seemed to spin in place. Historical figures who had formerly commanded armies and directed the movement of masses through wars, campaigns, and battles now guided the surging masses through political and diplomatic maneuvers, laws, and treaties.
Historians call this activity of historical figures "the reaction."

In describing this period, they sternly condemn the historical figures who, in their view, caused what they call the reaction. All the prominent people of that era—from Alexander and Napoleon to Madame de Stael, Photius, Schelling, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others—are arraigned before their stern tribunal and acquitted or condemned according to whether they promoted progress or reaction.

According to these accounts, a reaction took place in Russia too at this time, and the chief culprit was Alexander I—the same man who, according to these same historians, was the chief cause of the liberal reforms at the start of his reign, the savior of Russia, and the hero of Europe. Yet in present-day Russian literature, from schoolboy essayists to serious historians, there is no one who does not criticize Alexander for the things he supposedly did wrong during this period.
There is no one in Russian literature now, from schoolboy essayists to learned historians, who does not take a shot at Alexander for his mistakes during this phase of his reign.

"He should have acted this way, not that way. In this case he did well; in that case, badly. He was admirable at the start of his reign and during 1812, but was wrong to give a constitution to Poland, create the Holy Alliance, empower Arakcheyev, encourage Golitsyn and mysticism, and then encourage Shishkov and Photius. He was wrong to interfere with the army's front-line administration; he was wrong to disband the Semyonovsky regiment, and so on and so on."
It would take a dozen pages to list all the criticisms historians make of him, based on their knowledge of what is good for humanity.

Don't the very actions for which historians praise Alexander I—the liberal reforms at the start of his reign, the struggle with Napoleon, the firmness he showed in 1812, and the campaign of 1813—flow from the same sources, the same conditions of birth, education, and life that shaped Alexander's personality and produced the actions for which historians blame him, such as the Holy Alliance, the restoration of Poland, and the reaction of the 1820s?
What is the real substance of these criticisms?

It lies in the fact that a historical figure like Alexander I, standing at the highest possible pinnacle of human power, in the blinding light of history focused upon him—exposed to the strongest influences imaginable: the intrigues, flattery, and self-deception inseparable from power, and feeling a responsibility for everything happening in Europe at every moment of his life—proved to be, not fifty years ago but today, not a person of particularly virtuous character. That is what the historians' criticisms amount to.

But even if we assume that Alexander was mistaken fifty years ago in his idea of what was good for the people, we must also assume that the historian who judges him will, after some time, also turn out to be wrong in his understanding of what is good for humanity. This assumption is all the more natural and inevitable because the development of history shows us that every year, with every new writer, what we consider good for humanity changes. What once seemed good—giving Poland a constitution and forming the Holy Alliance—is later regarded as harmful. What seems harmful—the Napoleonic wars, the spread of revolutionary ideas—is later recognized as good.

Alexander's activity, or Napoleon's, cannot be called useful or harmful, because we cannot say what it was useful or harmful for. If someone dislikes it, that is only because it doesn't match their limited understanding of what is good. Whether I see the preservation of my father's house in Moscow in 1812 as good, or the glory of the Russian army, or the prosperity of Petersburg's university or Poland's freedom, or Russia's greatness, or Europe's balance of power, or a certain kind of European civilization called "progress"—I must acknowledge that the activity of any historical figure had, besides these aims, other aims more broadly and universally human that are beyond my grasp.

But let us suppose that what is called science can reconcile all contradictions and possesses an unchanging standard of good and bad by which to judge historical characters and events; let us say that Alexander could have done everything differently; let us even say that—guided by those who criticize him, who claim to know the ultimate goal of humanity's movement—he could have followed the program of nationalism, freedom, equality, and progress (for there seems to be no other) that his present-day critics would prescribe for him. Let us assume all that was possible. What then would have become of the activity of all the people who opposed the direction that the government was taking at that time? Their activity would not have existed; there would have been no life; there would have been nothing.
If we accept that human life can be governed by reason, then the very possibility of life is destroyed.
